summaries.headline: After Reading Reform, Districts Turn to Writing
summaries.summary: Colorado elementary schools are extending their science-of-reading overhaul into writing instruction, teaching explicit sentence and paragraph construction rather than assuming the skill develops naturally alongside reading. At Sand Creek Elementary, first graders who struggled to write a single sentence in the fall are now independently producing organized, multi-sentence paragraphs, with teachers reporting growth they haven't seen in previous years of teaching. The shift reflects a broader recognition among literacy experts that writing has lagged behind reading in curriculum reform, leaving a generation of students who can decode text but still struggle to construct one.

summaries.headline: Chronic Absenteeism Slows Pandemic Academic Recovery
summaries.summary: A new NWEA analysis of scores across 2,000 districts from 2019 to 2024 finds that districts with persistently high chronic absenteeism—20% or more of students missing at least 10% of school days—lagged furthest behind in returning to pre-pandemic achievement levels. The recovery gap was most pronounced in math, where high-absenteeism districts remained roughly 50% further from recovery than in reading, and the effect was strongest in the highest-poverty districts. The findings reinforce attendance as a lever tied directly to core academic outcomes, not a peripheral concern separate from instruction.

summaries.headline: Educator Views on SEL Hold Steady Since 2022
summaries.summary: Educator attitudes toward social-emotional learning have remained largely unchanged over the past four years, even as SEL became a flashpoint in political fights over DEI and critical race theory. EdWeek Research Center surveys show about half of educators still rate SEL's impact on academic outcomes and soft skills as "somewhat positive," a figure that has barely moved since the backlash began, though some districts quietly dropped the SEL label while keeping the practices. The steadiness suggests that political noise around SEL hasn't translated into meaningful shifts in how educators on the ground actually experience or value the work.

summaries.headline: Colorado Law Change Forces Second School Closure
summaries.summary: Pueblo Classical Academy, serving 260 K-12 students, will not reopen this fall after Colorado lawmakers moved to restrict the authorizing power of ERBOCES, a Monument-based education co-op that had authorized both the school and the now-closed Riverstone Academy. Lawmakers passed the restrictions late in the legislative session amid controversy over ERBOCES's expanding footprint authorizing homeschool enrichment programs statewide, forcing three affected schools to seek new authorizers; only Ascend College Prep succeeded, gaining charter status through the Charter School Institute, while Pueblo Classical's bid to join Pueblo School District 60 was rejected by the local board. The swift closures underscore how quickly a single legislative fix targeting one authorizer can ripple into real consequences for students and families, particularly when schools lack a fallback authorizing relationship.

summaries.headline: Memphis Ramps Up Attendance Push Amid Takeover
summaries.summary: Memphis-Shelby County Schools leaders and attendance staff are going door-to-door in high-absenteeism neighborhoods as part of a "Greatness At Your Door" campaign, the sixth such excursion since April, aiming to re-engage families and curb chronic absenteeism. More than 30% of MSCS students were chronically absent in 2024-25, missing 18 or more days, compared with 18.3% statewide, and the district's enrollment has dropped over 9% in the past decade versus 2.5% statewide. Chronic absenteeism was one of four factors cited in the state's now-contested takeover of MSCS, putting the district's on-the-ground outreach efforts under direct scrutiny as officials weigh whether local intervention can outpace state control.

summaries.headline: Retention Policies May Boost Reading Before Anyone's Held Back
summaries.summary: A new working paper from researchers at American University and Syracuse University finds that third-grade retention policies can improve reading outcomes even before any students are actually held back, suggesting the threat of retention itself changes school behavior. Eighteen states now have retention laws tied to reading proficiency, many enacted alongside "science of reading" legislation, and researchers point to the added instructional support and intervention systems these policies push schools to build as the likely driver of gains. The finding complicates a polarized debate where critics warn of social-emotional harm from holding students back and proponents argue the systemic pressure to intervene early outweighs those risks.

summaries.headline: AI Use Outpaces Educator and Parent Confidence
summaries.summary: A new Instructure survey of 1,125 U.S. respondents finds AI use in education has become routine even as guardrails lag behind adoption, with 90% of higher ed students, 68% of K-12 educators and 73% of parents reporting at least occasional classroom AI use. Parents in the survey acknowledged benefits like personalized learning and expanded access to resources, but voiced concern about students growing overly dependent on the technology and losing critical thinking skills. With usage now the norm rather than the exception, the pressure shifts to districts and institutions to build the oversight and instructional structures that determine whether AI strengthens learning or quietly erodes it.

summaries.headline: Cumberland County Treats Absenteeism as a Symptom, Not the Disease
summaries.summary: Leaders in North Carolina's Cumberland County Schools are reframing chronic absenteeism as a signal rather than a standalone problem, arguing that behind most missed-school patterns lies a mental health struggle, unstable housing, immigration-related fear, or a student who no longer believes anyone at school would notice their absence. Rather than escalating through letters and warnings toward disciplinary referrals, the district is building a proactive prevention framework centered on relationships, with staff trained to ask why a student is missing school and stay for the answer. The approach suggests that districts chasing attendance-rate targets through compliance measures alone are solving the wrong problem, while those investing in belonging and early outreach are addressing the one that actually drives the numbers.

summaries.headline: Aligning Vendor Contracts With District Outcomes
summaries.summary: District leaders increasingly face a mismatch between what vendors are paid to deliver and what schools actually need from a purchase, whether that's improved literacy scores, higher platform usage, or measurable gains in student outcomes. Outcomes-based contracting ties vendor payment or renewal to performance metrics defined upfront, shifting risk away from districts and forcing clearer conversations about what success looks like before ink hits paper. As procurement budgets tighten and scrutiny over edtech ROI grows, districts that build accountability into contracts—rather than relying on goodwill after the sale—put themselves in a stronger position to demand results.

summaries.headline: Michigan Governor Candidates Split on School Fixes
summaries.summary: Four remaining Michigan gubernatorial candidates—Democrats Jocelyn Benson and Chris Swanson, and Republicans John James and Perry Johnson—head into Aug. 4 primaries agreeing broadly on the need to improve literacy, career readiness, and teacher support, but diverge sharply beyond that, with Republicans emphasizing school choice and Democrats prioritizing equitable funding. The consensus comes against a grim backdrop: just 38.9% of Michigan third graders scored proficient on last year's state reading test, the lowest mark in the exam's 11-year history, with math scores similarly weak and NAEP results showing no recovery since before the pandemic. Candidates' plans remain long on broad goals and short on implementation specifics, leaving education leaders to parse rhetoric for signals on how state policy—and funding priorities—might shift depending on who wins in November.

summaries.headline: Edtech's English-First Design Leaves Families Behind
summaries.summary: Most learning platforms schools ask families to use are built English-first, leaving parents who speak another language at home unable to sit with their kids and help with schoolwork. The stakes are rising as states move to mandate personal finance instruction — California's Assembly Bill 2927 requires a stand-alone course for graduation starting with the class of 2030-31, with schools required to offer it by 2027-28 — meaning households already navigating financial literacy gaps may also be the least equipped to reinforce lessons at home. A graduation requirement built without multilingual access risks widening the same gaps it's meant to close.

summaries.headline: Data Governance Needs Leadership, Not Just IT
summaries.summary: District leaders are building formal data governance programs to protect student information, meet FERPA and COPPA requirements, and ensure data quality for AI and analytics, but documentation often lags behind actual practice. Wayland Public Schools technology director Jenn Judkins realized her team had strong informal privacy practices around access and vendor vetting that were never written down, a gap CoSN's Melissa Tebbenkamp says undermines training, enforcement and improvement over time. Tebbenkamp notes that many districts still treat governance as a pure IT function rather than a districtwide leadership responsibility, leaving even well-intentioned programs without the buy-in needed to make practices like least-privilege access and data minimization stick.

summaries.headline: CPS Furlough Plan Draws Teacher Backlash
summaries.summary: Chicago Public Schools teachers and the Chicago Teachers Union are pushing the Board of Education to reject a $9.88 billion budget proposal that includes all-staff furloughs and a spending freeze to close a $732.5 million deficit. The union estimates the furloughs, which would fall on professional development days, amount to a 2.3% pay cut, while teachers testified that layoffs already underway could push some class sizes to 47 students, violating contract limits, and left at least one school without adequate custodial support during a rodent infestation. CPS CEO Macquline King calls the plan "very painful" but says the board must approve it within ten days to ensure the district can make payroll this fall, leaving little room for revisions before the school year begins.

summaries.headline: California Locks In Permanent Farm-to-School Funding
summaries.summary: Governor Gavin Newsom has signed SB 172 into law, permanently funding California's farm-to-school program rather than leaving it subject to annual budget negotiations. The law is designed to increase local food sourcing in school meals and expand hands-on food education for students, building on the state's existing status as a national leader in farm-to-school investment. Permanent funding status shields the program from the budget cuts that have stalled similar initiatives in other states, giving districts a more stable foundation for long-term sourcing and curriculum planning.

summaries.headline: Newark Names 19 New District Leaders for Fall
summaries.summary: Newark Public Schools is installing nine new principals, five new directors, and five new assistant superintendents this fall, backfilling roles left open by a wave of retirements including longtime assistant superintendents Carolyn Granato, Sylvia Esteves, and Rosa Branco. Most incoming principals are homegrown talent — longtime district vice principals and educators — reflecting the district's multi-year push to build teacher-to-leader pipelines rather than recruit externally; this year's cohort follows six new principals in 2025, eight in 2024, and 10 in 2023. Annual turnover at this scale means Newark's leadership bench is being almost entirely rebuilt over a rolling four-year cycle, putting real weight behind the district's bet that growing leaders internally can sustain stability even as top posts change hands so frequently.

summaries.headline: Virtual School Teacher Wins Award, Rethinks STEM Access
summaries.summary: Jude Julien, a chemistry and earth science teacher who helped launch New York City's only fully virtual public high school four years ago, brought two decades of brick-and-mortar experience plus adjunct online teaching credentials to the Virtual Innovators Academy, which served more than 320 students last school year. His approach centers on treating STEM instruction as fundamentally personalized rather than standardized, an outlook that has earned him a Sloan Award, Big Apple Award semi-finalist status, and this year's Math for America Muller Award, carrying $20,000 for Julien and $5,000 for his school. As virtual and hybrid models become permanent fixtures in urban districts, Julien's recognition signals that equitable STEM access may depend less on the format of instruction and more on how deliberately educators adapt to individual student needs within it.

summaries.headline: Detroit School Board's Top Two Won't Seek Reelection
summaries.summary: Detroit's school board chair LaTrice McClendon and vice chair Corletta Vaughn both missed the July filing deadline for the November 3 election, with Vaughn disqualified over $950 in unpaid Wayne County fees and McClendon choosing not to refile despite being eligible after clearing a late fee from December 2025. Five of the board's seven seats are on this year's ballot, and with McClendon and Vaughn stepping aside, only Iris Taylor, Steve Bland Jr., and Bessie Harris have filed to retain their positions. The departure of both top officers, attributed partly to campaign paperwork lapses political consultants call common in Michigan races, leaves the district's governing body facing a leadership vacuum just as voters prepare to reshape its majority.

summaries.headline: Poorest Districts Have Outspent Wealthiest for Decades
summaries.summary: A Brookings analysis spanning nearly 50 years of Census Bureau data finds that high-poverty and predominantly non-white school districts have spent more per student on average than their wealthier, whiter counterparts across all 50 states. Lead author Sarah Reber notes that higher labor costs in many of these districts offset some of that spending advantage, but the underlying pattern still contradicts the widely held assumption that local property tax funding structurally shortchanges poor schools. The findings don't rule out a case for more funding, but they suggest that fixating on spending levels and allocation formulas may distract leaders and policymakers from other drivers of educational inequality.

summaries.headline: AI Policies Race Ahead, Data Privacy Lags
summaries.summary: AI use in K-12 classrooms surged in the past year, with RAND finding 54% of students and 53% of teachers using it for school, both up more than 15 percentage points, but formal policy has not kept pace, with only 45% of principals and 34% of teachers reporting a district AI policy at all. Ohio became the first state to mandate district AI policies by July 2026, and its model explicitly requires districts to address FERPA compliance and protection of student data, but adoption isn't universal and many districts nationally still have no policy framework to build privacy protections into. With federal law like FERPA not built for AI-era data training and recent breaches at vendors like PowerSchool and Canvas exposing student records, districts writing policy now are setting precedent for how much scrutiny data privacy gets versus acceptable-use rules alone.

summaries.headline: Supreme Court Pushes CBSE Toward Real Data Consent
summaries.summary: India's Supreme Court has signaled it will order CBSE to revise the consent form for its Aadhaar-linked APAAR student ID system, explicitly requiring an opt-out option for parents. The move comes amid a writ petition from parents of four students who argue the current scheme functions as compelled enrollment and fails to meet standards under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, prompting the Court to also direct CBSE to address how student data is protected and processed. The case adds to a growing pattern of courts and regulators scrutinizing whether large-scale education data systems are built with genuine consent or just the appearance of it.

by: Carolina Hauger

Posted: Jul 22, 2026 / 05:46 PM CDT

Updated: Jul 22, 2026 / 05:49 PM CDT

SHARE

AUSTIN (Nexstar) — A West Texas school district will challenge Texas’ school finance system in a lawsuit that argues the state has too much control over local property taxes.

The Midland ISD Board of Trustees voted Tuesday to authorize a [lawsuit](https://midlandisd.community.diligentoneplatform.com/document/22bce204-4065-4c81-862d-e3146070ec7f/) against the State of Texas and Texas Education Commissioner Mike Morath. The case would ask a Travis County court to determine whether the state’s school funding system violates the Texas Constitution by limiting local control over property taxes and creating a state property tax.

### What does the lawsuit argue?

The lawsuit argues the Texas Legislature has shifted control over local school property taxes to the state. It claims that, because of changes made under [House Bill 3](https://capitol.texas.gov/billlookup/BillSummary.aspx?LegSess=86R&Bill=HB3) in 2019, local school boards no longer have meaningful discretion over setting maintenance and operations tax rates or deciding how much of tax revenue they can keep.

The lawsuit contends school districts have become “mere tax collectors” for the state and that Commissioner Morath “is sued solely in his official capacity as the state official responsible for administering the Foundation School Program and calculating and publishing each school district’s Maximum Compressed Rate under Tier One of the Foundation School Program.”

Midland ISD also argues that the Legislature effectively creates a statewide property tax, which [Article 8 Section 24](https://tcss.legis.texas.gov/resources/cn/pdf/cn.8.pdf) of the Texas Constitution prohibits. It also argues voters never directly approved the mandatory Tier One maintenance and operations tax created under state law.

Mary Lynn Pruneda, director of education and workforce policy at Texas 2036, said previous Texas Supreme Court decisions upheld earlier versions of the recapture system, finding they did not constitute a statewide property tax.

Under Texas’ recapture system, commonly known as “Robin Hood,” districts with higher property values must send a portion of their locally collected property taxes back to the state. The money is then redistributed to districts with lower property values to help equalize school funding across Texas.

Pruneda said the purpose of recapture is to help provide students across Texas with a more equitable education by redistributing excess local revenue from property-wealthy districts.

“The state of Texas has an interest in providing an equal public education for students… in every single corner of the state,” Pruneda said.

### Why Midland?

The school district sits in the oil-rich Permian Basin, where valuable oil and gas properties generate substantial local property tax revenue. Because of those high property values, the state classifies Midland ISD as a “property-wealthy” district.

According to the lawsuit, Midland ISD expects to collect about $313 million in local maintenance and operations property taxes this year. About $83 million, roughly one-quarter of that revenue, would be sent back to the state through recapture. The district says it has contributed more than $1 billion through the program since 2013.

### Does Midland receive state funding?

Midland ISD, like every public school district in Texas, receives funding through the Foundation School Program, Texas’ primary system for funding public schools. This program allocates state money to districts based on various factors, including student enrollment, student needs and local property tax revenue.

However, because Midland ISD’s local property tax collections exceed the amount the state says it needs to educate its students, the district sends substantially more money back through recapture than it receives in direct state aid.

### Is the lawsuit connected to Midland’s population growth?

Not directly.

The lawsuit focuses primarily on property values, not population growth.

Still, Midland ISD argues growth creates additional challenges. As the Permian Basin continues to expand, the district says it must build schools, hire teachers and serve more students. At the same time, increasing property values also increase the amount of local tax revenue subject to recapture.

District leaders argue that means local taxpayers are contributing more while local school officials have less authority over how those dollars are ultimately used.

### What happens next?

Midland ISD filed the lawsuit in Travis County on Wednesday.

If the lawsuit succeeds, it would not automatically eliminate the recapture system. Instead, a court could require the Texas Legislature to redesign portions of the state’s school finance system while maintaining constitutional requirements for funding public education.

Pruneda said she hopes the legal challenge does not overshadow broader issues facing Texas schools.

“We get so focused on these lawsuits,” she said, “that we lose sight of the fact that only 50% of kids can read and do math on grade level. I just wish that we took half of the energy that we take into talking about school finance and put that energy into working together … to figure out how we get our kids back on grade level.”

KXAN has reached out to Mike Morath for comment but has not heard back.

Midland ISD will sue Texas officials over the state’s so-called Robin Hood funding system for public schools, a significant attempt at forcing lawmakers to revisit how they go about ensuring low-income campuses benefit from resources similar to those that wealthier campuses enjoy.

The West Texas school trustees voted unanimously Tuesday to proceed with a lawsuit against Education Commissioner Mike Morath and state leaders, arguing that funding restrictions imposed by the Legislature prohibit them from raising and spending money to meet the needs of their students.

“We can sit here on this stage, and we can complain about it,” Midland ISD Board President Josh Guinn said before the vote. But nothing changes, Guinn added, “until you have four people — elected school board members — in the state of Texas say, ‘Enough’s enough. You’re going to stop stealing our community’s money.’”

Guinn said in an interview that he expected the district to file the lawsuit by 5 p.m. Wednesday but could not yet confirm whether it occurred. Texas Education Agency officials declined to comment on Midland’s decision to sue.

Frustrations over funding include a decades-old state mandate known as recapture in which districts in wealthy communities relinquish excess dollars raised locally to districts that struggle to generate property tax revenue. Recapture has survived at least three legal challenges in the last 30 years — in 1995, 2005 and 2016, respectively.

Located in a community rich in oil and gas, Midland will pay the state more than $83 million for recapture this school year, according to the [lawsuit draft](https://midlandisd.community.diligentoneplatform.com/document/22bce204-4065-4c81-862d-e3146070ec7f/). That represents 27% of the district’s $313 million generated locally.

Property taxes make up the majority of public school funding, while state dollars generally fill remaining gaps along with some federal aid.

The Midland school trustees contend that recent changes to Texas’ education funding system, dating back to 2019, unfairly deprived local communities of decision-making power over how they tax residents, instead granting much of that authority to the education commissioner.

Rather than allowing local school boards to set taxes within a certain range determined by the state, districts do so at the rate decided by the commissioner or risk losing state funding, they argue. Meanwhile, state leaders imposed requirements on how districts spend money raised locally, which the Midland trustees say prevents them from addressing their particular needs. Local needs vary across Texas’ more than 1,200 districts, they note.

Texas’ recapture system, often called Robin Hood, was enacted in 1993 after underfunded schools — led by the predominantly Hispanic and low-income Edgewood district in San Antonio — sued the state over substantial disparities in resources between their children and those attending school in wealthier communities.

Back then, recapture mostly affected wealthy suburban and oil-rich districts. In 1994, [34 school districts](https://txsc.org/issues-in-focus-recapture/) redistributed funding through the system, according to the Texas School Coalition.

Now, hundreds of districts — including those in major urban communities with declining enrollment and high numbers of students in poverty — pay more in recapture because of their local economies’ growth. The Austin school district — one of the largest in Texas — reported paying [roughly $8.3 billion](https://austincurrent.org/2026/04/20/texas-austin-aisd-school-budget-finance-deficit/) through recapture between 2000 and 2025.

Midland is among the top 10 districts in Texas sending money back to the state for recapture, according to education agency data.

Rather than using recapture as a tool for educational equity, the Midland trustees argue that state leaders use it in place of funding schools properly. They say recapture does not account for the fact that more than half of the district’s students qualify for free or reduced-price lunch, which the state and federal governments consider a measure of poverty.

“Property wealth is not educational wealth. You cannot teach a child with a mineral appraisal,” Midland ISD trustee Matt Friez said Tuesday. “You need a teacher standing in front of the child. The recapture formula sees the minerals beneath our feet and does not adequately see what it costs out here in Midland to hire and retain a great teacher above them.”

When the Texas Supreme Court found recapture constitutional in 2016, it noted that lawmakers still needed to make improvements to public school funding. More than two-thirds of districts had sued in that case.

School administrators have since argued that state leaders have not prioritized investments in traditional neighborhood campuses but instead pushed to grow charter schools and create a voucher program that allows families to use public funding for private or home schooling.

When lawmakers approved funding changes in recent years, they did so with [more restrictions](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/07/03/texas-public-education-funding-house-bill-2/) on how districts could spend the money, arguing that schools had not focused enough on improving student outcomes.

“They’re setting the tax rate. We collect the taxes. We send it to the state,” Guinn, the Midland school board president, said Wednesday. “Then we get blamed as a local district and local board member for taxes being high. It’s just a revolving door.”

It is unclear whether additional school districts will join Midland’s lawsuit.

The legal challenge from Midland, a community that reliably votes Republican, comes as top GOP state leaders such as [Gov. Greg Abbott](https://directory.texastribune.org/greg-abbott/) push to [abolish school property taxes](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/12/09/greg-abbott-schools-property-tax-cut-election-2026/). Kevin O’Hanlon and Kara Belew will represent the West Texas district in the lawsuit, according to the draft filing.

O’Hanlon represented the Texas Attorney General’s Office in Edgewood v. Kirby — the landmark school finance case that led to the creation of recapture. Belew has served as statewide budget director for Abbott, as one of the Texas Education Agency’s top finance experts and as a senior policy adviser for the conservative Texas Public Policy Foundation.

A new legal challenge to Texas’ school funding system renews questions about what methods state leaders should use to ensure students in low-income districts and those attending campuses in more affluent communities receive an education on a level playing field.

The Midland school district voted to sue Education Commissioner Mike Morath and state leaders this week, focusing on a piece of Texas’ school finance system known as recapture or “Robin Hood.” Texas courts have repeatedly found recapture in compliance with the state constitution — in 1995, 2005 and 2016, respectively.

But the latest challenge from West Texas represents decades-long frustrations Texas schools hold with state leaders’ approach to paying for public education. Despite new dollars approved last year, many districts have closed schools, shuttered programs and cut staffing in response to a funding crisis they say the Legislature helped cause.

Here’s what to know.

## **What is recapture?**

Recapture, often referred to as “Robin Hood,” passed into law in 1993 after the predominantly Hispanic and low-income Edgewood school district and dozens of other underfunded campuses sued Texas over significant disparities between the resources students in their communities received and kids who attended school in affluent neighborhoods.

Under recapture, school districts that receive more local property tax revenue than their state-determined need must send excess funds back to the state. The state then redirects that money to districts that struggle to generate local funding.

During the 2024–25 fiscal year — the most recent with finalized data — 225 districts sent nearly $3 billion back to the state, according to data from the Texas Education Agency. That’s up from just over $1.4 billion a decade prior.

## **How much is recapture costing districts?**

As districts’ local economies have grown, so has their property wealth — resulting in more districts sending money back to the state.

In 1994 — the year after recapture passed into law — 34 school districts redistributed $131 million through the system, many of them in Texas’ wealthy suburbs, according to the Texas School Coalition, an organization advocating on behalf of recapture districts.

Since then, districts have sent roughly $45.5 billion in total recapture funds to the state — including those located in urban communities with high numbers of students in low-income households as well as from oil-rich areas.

Austin ISD sent more than $770 million back to the state during the 2024-25 school year, by far the most of any district. Austin has led the state in recapture payments for nearly 20 consecutive years, according to the coalition. Slightly less than half of the district’s students come from low-income households, though the number of children learning English and kids with dyslexia rank high above state averages.

West Texas’ Pecos-Barstow-Toyah ISD paid roughly $198 million, the second-largest amount. The Midland school district, which recently sued the state, paid the sixth-most at $92.4 million. Houston ISD, the largest district in Texas, paid the tenth-most at $55.5 million.

## **What are arguments for and against recapture?**

Some property-wealthy districts argue that because Texas counts recapture as part of its funding contribution to public schools, elected state leaders use it not as a tool to improve resources for low-income students but rather as an excuse to avoid funneling additional money to the children most in need.

Frustrations with recapture are underscored by the reality that many Texas districts are sending money back to the state as they close schools, cut programs and navigate staffing shortages.

But without recapture, advocates fear, schools in property-wealthy districts would receive significantly more funding to educate their students than those in areas with low property values, potentially leaving underserved children worse off.

Some public education advocates argue that the problem is not with recapture but with inconsistent and unreliable state funding. Prior to the 2025 legislative session, for example, Texas schools endured six years without a boost to the pot of money schools can use to raise teacher salaries and cover operational expenses.

## **What is Midland ISD arguing in its lawsuit?**

Located in a community rich in oil and gas, Midland will pay the state more than $83 million for recapture this school year, according to a draft of the legal filing. That represents 27% of the district’s $313 million generated locally.

Midland has consistently ranked top 10 in recapture districts over the last decade, according to the Texas School Coalition.

Midland school trustees contend that recent changes to Texas’ education funding system, dating back to 2019, unfairly deprived local communities of decision-making power over how they tax residents, instead granting much of that authority to the education commissioner.

Rather than allowing local school boards to set taxes within a certain range determined by the state, districts do so at the rate decided by the commissioner or risk losing state funding, they argue. Meanwhile, state lawmakers continue to impose requirements on how districts spend money raised locally, which the Midland trustees say prevents them from addressing their community’s particular needs.

Roughly 68% of the district’s students are Hispanic, while nearly 55% qualify for free or reduced-price lunch — the latter of which the state and federal governments consider a measure of poverty. The trustees argue that the number of students who come from low-income households shows that property wealth does not necessarily equate to educational wealth.

## **What is the broader political context?**

State leaders have allocated tens of billions of dollars toward reducing the annual tax bill homeowners and businesses pay each year. They have also imposed tighter limits on how much local governments can increase taxes to pay for services such as public safety and parks.

The legal challenge to recapture from Midland, a community that reliably votes Republican, comes as top GOP leaders such as [Gov. Greg Abbott](https://directory.texastribune.org/greg-abbott/) now push to [abolish school property taxes](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/12/09/greg-abbott-schools-property-tax-cut-election-2026/). Several Texas House lawmakers and prominent conservative groups have embraced the approach, though finance experts warn doing so would prove costly and appears unrealistic.

Property taxes make up the majority of public school funding, while state dollars generally fill remaining gaps along with some federal aid.

Attorneys Kevin O’Hanlon and Kara Belew, meanwhile, will represent Midland ISD in the recapture lawsuit.

O’Hanlon represented the Texas Attorney General’s Office in Edgewood v. Kirby — the landmark school finance case that led to the creation of recapture. Belew has served as statewide budget director for Abbott, as one of the Texas Education Agency’s top finance experts and as a senior policy adviser for the conservative Texas Public Policy Foundation.

# Letter: Dunleavy’s arithmetic of neglect and a temporary bridge to stronger school funding

By Gregg Brelsford

Published: July 18, 2026

For nearly eight years, Gov. Mike Dunleavy has presided over what many educators and school officials describe as the chronic underfunding of Alaska’s K–12 public schools. Across the eight school years touched by his tenure, Alaska’s public schools have recorded roughly 1 million student-years of enrollment.

Before the Legislature enacted a permanent Base Student Allocation increase for fiscal year 2026, the statutory BSA had risen only $30 during Dunleavy’s tenure, from $5,930 to $5,960 — a total increase of about one-half of 1%. During roughly the same period, consumer prices in urban Alaska rose by about 22%, substantially eroding the purchasing power of the state’s education funding formula. The Legislature later enacted a permanent $700 BSA increase for fiscal year 2026 over the governor’s veto.

For the coming school year, the governor initially proposed fully funding the existing $6,660 statutory BSA but did not propose an additional increase. Then, on June 24, he signed a budget leaving intact a provision that could provide up to $115 million in additional one-time energy relief funding, contingent on sufficient surplus revenue associated with the temporary oil-price spike caused by the Iran war. The revenue commissioner is scheduled to determine the amount available on Aug. 31.

Alaska simply cannot build a thriving, successful state without adequately educating the workers, citizens, entrepreneurs and leaders who will shape our future over the next 10 to 20 years.

The conditional one-time aid offers a measure of hope. It can serve as a bridge to a new era of sustained, full funding for Alaska’s K–12 public schools — not one built on a temporary oil windfall, but delivered by a future governor with the vision and determination to transform this temporary bridge into a permanent highway to educational excellence.

_**— Gregg Brelsford**_ _, Anchorage_

Mesa County Valley School District 51 Superintendent Brian Hill shows off his “Fund Public Schools” shirt while advocating for Colorado voters to pass Proposition NN during a rally with educators and advocates at Rocky Mountain Elementary School in Clifton on Tuesday, July 21.
Photo by NATHAN DEAL/The Daily Sentinel

A ballot measure that would increase state K-12 funding by more than 50% over a decade and address teacher pay will go before Colorado voters this autumn — and it’s already receiving vocal support from Western Slope education leaders and educators.

Several dozen education leaders, educators and advocates attended a rally Tuesday morning at Rocky Mountain Elementary School in Clifton in support of Proposition NN, the ballot measure that would, if passed, invest in teacher pay and retention, smaller class sizes, and career and technical education. The measure does not raise taxes on Coloradans or change any tax bracket. Included in the ballot measure is an annual independent audit to prove the money is being spent entirely on designated purposes.

Speakers at the rally included Mesa County Valley School District 51 Superintendent Brian Hill, Mesa Valley Educators Association (MVEA) President Stephanie Walker and Colorado Education Association (CEA) Vice President Liz Waddick. D51 Board of Education President Jose Luis Chávez and Board Member Kaci Cole were also in attendance, though they did not speak and the board has not officially taken a stance on the ballot measure.

![MVEA Prop NN](https://bloximages.newyork1.vip.townnews.com/gjsentinel.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/4/aa/4aa5e299-887b-4332-aa8e-a19952487b28/6a5fed153b75a.image.jpg)

Photo by NATHAN DEAL/The Daily Sentinel

Mesa Valley Educators Association (MVEA) President Stephanie Walker speaks during a pro-Prop NN rally with educators and advocates Tuesday, July 21, 2026, at Rocky Mountain Elementary School in Clifton.
Photo by NATHAN DEAL/The Daily Sentinel

Hill went through statistics from independent studies commissioned by state legislators, with Colorado ranking 43rd out of 50 states in school funding, 41st in teacher pay and 50th in teacher wage competitiveness, all while housing costs continue to rise. He said Prop NN, if passed, would have a “direct positive impact on District 51” in terms of teacher recruitment and retention, faster intervention for struggling students, better relationships between students and teachers, and more opportunities for students.

“I love living in our state, and Colorado has so much to be proud of, but public education funding is not one of those things.... D51 does compete for teachers with districts on the Front Range and in other states that can pay more. When we can’t offer competitive pay, we lose good teachers and our students feel that loss first-hand. It isn’t abstract for us. It’s the difference between a crowded classroom and a classroom where teachers can provide individualized support for kids, or whether a student in Fruita or Palisade or Grand Junction has access to career and technical education that leads straight into a good local job. The truth is that Colorado has never adequately funded public education, and it’s time for all of us as Coloradans to step up,” Hill said.

![Prop NN](https://bloximages.newyork1.vip.townnews.com/gjsentinel.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/d/a1/da11b548-f23f-4246-b163-3cc2b19e0715/6a5fecbf95320.image.jpg)

More than two dozen supporters of Proposition NN, including speaker Liz Waddick (Colorado Education Association Vice President, center) and Mesa County Valley School District 51 Superintendent Brian Hill (in black to the right) attend a rally Tuesday, July 21, 2026, at Rocky Mountain Elementary School in Clifton.
Photo by NATHAN DEAL/The Daily Sentinel

“We aren’t asking for the moon. We’re asking for the opportunity for our students to be amongst the stars. That requires adequate funding, and Prop NN would help get us closer to that.”

Walker agreed that the proposition would bolster the district’s standing with prospective and tenured educators. She added that a D51-backed mill levy override with similar goals will also be on Mesa County voters’ ballots in November.

“This fall, there will also be another opportunity to support education with our mill levy override. District 51 ranks 12th out of 13 of our peer districts when it comes to MLO dollars per student. Mill levy override funding supports programs and teacher salaries and helps close the gap when state funding comes up short,” Walker said.

![GJHS Prop NN](https://bloximages.newyork1.vip.townnews.com/gjsentinel.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/7/d6/7d623a0e-a604-4570-8e47-0f64fddb51d7/6a5fed6122da6.image.jpg)

Grand Junction High School science teacher Cleon Hodges speaks during a pro-Prop NN rally with educators and advocates Tuesday, July 21, 2026, at Rocky Mountain Elementary School in Clifton.
Photo by NATHAN DEAL/The Daily Sentinel

“D51 hasn’t asked the community for an MLO tax increase since 2017. The 2026 mill levy override dollars will go toward supporting getting teacher pay closer to market. Even with the work that we’ve done to boost teacher pay over the past few years, we still rank last among our peer districts in starting teacher pay.”

Waddick went over more statistics from independent studies, showing that the state’s chronic underfunding of K-12 education amounts to $4,600 per student.

“Take a second to imagine what you want for Colorado kids, what you want for your own children, for your neighbor’s children, for our children,” Waddick said.

Other speakers included Palisade High School business and computer science teacher and Future Business Leaders of America (FBLA) adviser Melissa Wright as well as Grand Junction High School science teacher Cleon Hodges. Both said that costs of housing and living make it difficult for quality teachers to stay in their positions, with Hodges adding that he sometimes has to eliminate lab activities for safety reasons if there are too many students in the class.

# York supervisors place school funding tax referendum on November ballot

By

[Ben Martindale](mailto: info@wydaily.com)

YORK COUNTY – The York County Board of Supervisors voted Tuesday night to approve a resolution placing a School Capital Funding Referendum on the November ballot, allowing voters to decide whether the county may implement a dedicated 1% local sales and use tax for school construction and major renovation projects.

The referendum does not enact the tax but allows voters to decide whether the county may implement it. The Virginia General Assembly recently gave counties and cities the ability to ask voters to approve a local sales and use tax dedicated solely to school construction and major renovation projects

If approved by voters, the measure is estimated to generate about $12 million annually, according to county officials. The referendum will appear on the November general election ballot.

Also during Tuesday’s meeting, county officials also provided an update on the Penniman Road Corridor Rehabilitation Project, which will identify residents in need of assistance and rehabilitate their homes.

A study conducted by York County sent surveys to 882 residents in the area. Of the 194 people who responded, 110 indicated they were interested in and qualified for assistance. The first project area will be York Terrace Northwest.

York County has requested a $1.5 million grant for the project and committed a $75,450 local match. The grant application was submitted July 1, with a decision expected in the fall.

The board also voted 4-1, with District 2 representative Sheila Knoll dissenting, to table discussion of a proposed zoning ordinance amendment that would allow residents to use  cargo units as storage sheds.

Supervisors expressed differing opinions on the proposal, with Vice Chairman and District 5 Supervisor Thomas G. Shepperd Jr. among those raising concerns about allowing cargo units as accessory structures.

“I feel almost personally embarrassed that York County could be known as a place where you can turn a trailer into a storage unit,” said Shepperd. “Rubs me the wrong way.”

Further discussion is scheduled for the board’s next meeting on Sept. 15.

--:-- | COLUMBUS— The Polk County Board of Commissioners approved several items related to county operations, emergency management, schools and disaster recovery during its regular meeting Monday, July 20, at the Bryant H. Womack Justice and Administration Building. Among the board’s actions was scheduling a public hearing for Aug. 17 to consider a proposed amendment to the county’s zoning ordinance regarding residential short-term vacation rentals in the Hunting Country Rd. area. Planning Administrator Chelsea Louray told commissioners the Planning Board found the request to be consistent with the county’s comprehensive plan but recommended against approving the amendment because of opposition expressed by residents in the area. The proposed amendment would allow residential vacation rentals by right in the Residential Estate zoning district. Commissioners also approved transferring $146,252.84 from the county’s Capital Reserve Account to reimburse Polk County Schools for capital expenditures. A Polk County Schools representative said the funding will replace approximately 345 aging student Chromebooks that have exceeded their expected service life. He said the purchase is part of establishing a sustainable device replacement cycle while reducing the district’s overall inventory to a more manageable level. The board approved a $1.37 million purchase order with Republic Services for annual landfill trash hauling and disposal services. County Manager Marche Pittman said the request represents the county’s routine annual contract for transporting and disposing of solid waste. Emergency Management Director Bobby Arledge presented two requests that received unanimous approval. ## Sign up for our daily email newsletter Get the latest news sent to your inbox The first authorizes the purchase and installation of additional flood gauges throughout Polk County using a state grant of more than $90,000. Arledge said the gauges will improve the county’s ability to monitor water levels during flood events and will be installed at approved bridge locations across the county. Commissioners also approved a memorandum of agreement with North Carolina Emergency Management to acquire four flood-prone properties through the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program. The acquisitions include one property in Tryon and three in Saluda. Arledge said the projects should move through the process more efficiently than previous acquisitions because they present fewer environmental challenges. Finance Director Sonya Ayers presented amendments to the county’s state disaster-response cash-flow loans, which commissioners approved unanimously. The amendments extend repayment deadlines for approximately $3.6 million in interest-free loans the county received following Hurricane Helene while awaiting reimbursement from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. Ayers said the amendments do not authorize additional borrowing or increase the loan amounts but instead provide greater repayment flexibility under recently enacted state legislation. Commissioners also filled several vacancies on county advisory boards. Sofia Lilly was appointed to the Agricultural Advisory Board, Katie Biel to the Economic and Tourism Development Commission, Cynthia Fowler, Jeremy Gregg and Pat Linnon to the Fire Rescue Advisory Committee, Christine Davis to the Health and Human Services Agency Board, and Linnon to the Recycling Advisory Board. During public comments, several residents again expressed opposing views on the county’s building of the YMCA, with supporters encouraging commissioners to move forward and opponents raising concerns about the project’s long-term financial impact and use of taxpayer funds. Following the commissioner’s comments, the board entered closed session regarding the attorney-client privilege before adjourning. The Polk County Board of Commissioners will hold its next regular meeting at 5 p.m. Monday, August 17, at the Bryant H. Womack Justice and Administration Building in Columbus. 02:38 | **By VDC staff** Across Vermont, many communities are grappling with rising education costs, declining enrollment, and growing concern about long-term affordability and outcomes. While legislators continue to debate possible reforms, a small ad hoc group of concerned citizens is beginning an effort to bring one specific question directly to Vermont voters through Town Meeting Day 2027, co-organizer Matthew Kelly of Milton said. The non-binding initiative asks whether Vermont should move toward a student-centered education funding system in which education dollars follow each child rather than being allocated primarily to school districts. The proposed advisory article reads: Shall the voters of the Town of **_\_\__** urge the Governor, the Vermont General Assembly, and Vermont’s congressional delegation to enact legislation establishing a student-centered education funding system in which state education dollars follow each child rather than being allocated primarily to school districts, thereby allowing parents or legal guardians to direct those funds toward an approved public school, independent school, career and technical education program, homeschooling expenses, microschool, or other state-approved educational option that best meets the needs of their child, while ensuring every Vermont child continues to have access to a quality education? Under Vermont law, registered voters may petition to place advisory articles on their Town Meeting warning if they meet the applicable petition requirements and filing deadlines. The Vermont Secretary of State provides guidance and sample petition forms for this process, and municipalities must follow the statutory procedures governing voter-backed petitions. “The purpose of this initiative isn’t to eliminate public education or to diminish Vermont’s commitment to ensuring every child has access to a quality education,” Kelly said. “Rather, it asks whether the state’s education funding model should place students and families at the center of the system by allowing funding to follow each child to an approved educational setting that best meets that student’s needs.” Supporters believe that Town Meeting Day offers Vermonters a unique opportunity to express their views directly. If the advisory article appears on ballots in communities across the state and receives broad support, the results could provide legislators with a clear indication of public sentiment as they consider future education reforms, Kelly said. ### Share this: -
